topic: Coldest permanently inhabited place: Oymyakon, Sakha Republic, Russia — −67.7 °C on 6 February 1933 (WMO-recognised northern-hemisphere record); ~500 residents; January mean about −46 °C; school closes below −52 °C (grades 1–5), older pupils below −56 °C; Vostok −89.2 °C is the planet's record (uninhabited station).
policy_note: Every spoken or shown fact → a claim with ≥ 2 independent publishers; core claims need a primary/scholarly source.

myths.myth: Canada or Greenland must be coldest because they are nearer the pole.
myths.reality: Oymyakon sits in a Siberian valley basin that traps draining cold air; the continental interior gets colder than coastal Arctic Canada or Greenland's inhabited coast.

claims.text: The coldest permanently inhabited place on Earth is Oymyakon in the Sakha Republic, Russia, where −67.7 °C was recorded on 6 February 1933.
vo: the coldest inhabited place on earth is in which country
russia. a tiny village deep in eastern siberia dropped below minus 67 degrees back in 1933

claims.text: About 500 people live in Oymyakon; the January daily mean is about −46 °C.
vo: around 500 people still live there today, and a perfectly normal january averages minus 46

claims.text: A household freezer runs at −18 °C; the lowest temperature measured on Earth is −89.2 °C at Vostok Station, Antarctica (21 July 1983).
vo: your kitchen freezer sits at minus 18. only antarctica goes colder, minus 89 at vostok station

claims.text: Oymyakon's school stays open until −52 °C for the youngest pupils; older pupils attend until −56 °C.
vo: and the school stays open until minus 52. the older pupils keep going until minus 56
